title: TensorRT v7/v8 using more GPU memory per model than v6, diffrence in createExecutionContext() API call
author: hrenek
body: Description I am using TensorRT C++ API to load multiple models. I'm migrating our codebase to TensorRT v7/v8 from v6 and I've noticed that there is a substantially more of GPU memory used per model. This results in application failing to load some the models on the same hardware it works on TFv6 due to out of GPU memory errors. Model files are completely the same no difference between versions. I've observed it for all models tried. Using the onnx or uff format, explicit or implict batch dimension, multiple configurations of workspace size, using IAlgorithmSelector to select different layer implementations seems to have no influence on this memory overhead. I've tracked memory overhead to the nvinfer1::ICudaEngine::createExecutionContext() API call. On TRT v6 it allocates exactly getDeviceMemorySize() and createExecutionContextWithoutDeviceMemory() allocates zero bytes of GPU memory. On TRT v7/v8 createExecutionContext() allocates more than getDeviceMemorySize() and createExecutionContextWithoutDeviceMemory() allocates more than zero bytes, roughly the size of the observed overhead increase per model. I'm testing the memory usage by looking at nvidia-smi output after each API call. Here are some stats on the typical models we use. Small retina net model. Object recognition model (inception resnet) and a larger object recognition model.    Mem usage Small retina TRTv6 Small retina TRTv7 Obj recog v6 Obj recog v7 Large obj recog v6 Large obj recog v7     Serialized model on disk 3,1 MB 4,5 MB 95 MB 91,5 MB 288 MB 288 MB   Observed overhead per model 21 MB 41 MB 247 MB 347 MB 947MB 1164 MB   TRTv7-TRTv8 difference --- 20 MB --- 100 MB --- 217 MB   getDeviceMemorySize() 11 MB 12 MB 140 MB 137 MB 650 MB 612 MB   createExecutionContext() overhead 11 MB 32 MB 140 MB 243 MB 651 MB 868 MB   TRTv7 log Allocated persistent device memory of size --- 3 MB --- 91,5 MB --- 250 MB   TRTv7 log Allocated activation device memory of size --- 12,9 MB --- 143,7 MB --- 642.3 MB    Observed numbers are for the whole model with input output buffer allocations after multiple model initializations so that everything is warm. TrtV7 log rows are what what createExecutionContext() outputs in the log. From the above numbers additional overhead track loosely to the size of the model but not perfectly. My best guess is that the weights are duplicated in the execution context+ some more stuff. This is observed on Windows and Linux on mulitple GPUs. The numbers above are from Windows 10, GTX 1080 ti card. body: Description  Running trtexec --onnx=./output.onnx --verbose gets segfault on the above model. The model file is attached, and can be generated with pytorch: import numpy as np import onnx import onnx.checker   inputs = {     # 'i1': np.random.rand(1, 1, 1, 1).astype(np.float32),     # 'i2': np.random.rand(1, 1, 1, 1).astype(np.float32), } import torch   class Model(torch.nn.Module):     def __init__(self) -> None:         super().__init__()         self.prelu = torch.nn.PReLU()         self.c = torch.nn.Parameter(             torch.rand(1, 1, 1, 1), requires_grad=False)      @torch.no_grad()     def forward(self):         o10 = self.prelu(self.c)         o10 = o10.mean(axis=0)         return (o10 > 0,)   model = Model() model.eval() torch_inp = {k: torch.from_numpy(v) for k, v in inputs.items()} torch.onnx.export(     model, tuple(torch_inp.values()),     "output.onnx", input_names=list(inputs.keys()),     verbose=False, opset_version=10)  onnx_model = onnx.load("output.onnx") onnx.checker.check_model(onnx_model) Sorry for the weird-looking model. title: Importing tensorrt causes Process finished with exit code -1073741819 (0xC0000005)
author: andrearosasco
body: Description  When I run the following code: from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation as R from torch import cdist import open3d as o3d  import tensorrt  import torch from configs import server_config from model import PCRNetwork   # # Load model model = PCRNetwork.load_from_checkpoint('./checkpoint/final', config=server_config.ModelConfig) model.cuda() model.eval()  x = torch.ones((1, 2024, 3)).cuda() torch.onnx.export(model.backbone, x, 'pcr.onnx', input_names=['input'], output_names=['output'], opset_version=11) I get the error: Process finished with exit code -1073741819 (0xC0000005)  returned while executing the last line of code. But if I move any of the first three imports below import tensorrt everything works and the onnx file is created. The error happens somewher inside torch.onnx.export. The exact line of code that causes the error is line 440 in torch/onnx/utils.py: graph_inputs = list(graph.inputs()) when they try to convert the iterator returned by graph.inputs() to a list. It appears to be a memory error but I don't understand how tensorrt causes it and why it does that only if those three precise imports precede it. Environment TensorRT Version: TensorRT-8.2.3.0.Windows10.x86_64.cuda-10.2.cudnn8.2 NVIDIA GPU: GeForce GTX 1650 Ti NVIDIA Driver Version: 30.0.14.9649 CUDA Version: 10.2 CUDNN Version: 8.2.1.32 (also tried 8.2.4.15) Operating System: Windows 10 Python Version (if applicable): 3.7 PyTorch Version (if applicable): 1.10.1 Baremetal or Container (if so, version): Baremetal Steps To Reproduce git clone https://github.com/andrearosasco/pcr.git switch to the branch train_box the file export_onnx.py contains the code shown in the snippet above and can be executed to reproduce the problem Additional FIles This is the output of print(graph)  graph.txt When I run the code without tensorrt the list(graph.inputs()) line just run instantaneously and return a list of 138 values.

author: the-final
body: Description [optimizer.cpp::computeCosts::2011] Error Code 10: Internal Error (Could not find any implementation for node conv1.weight + QuantizeLinear_7_quantize_scale_node + (Unnamed Layer* 14) [Shuffle] + Conv_9 + PWN(LeakyRelu_10).) if set  input shape (1, 256, 1000), error if set  input shape (1, 256, 100), worked fine increase config.max_workspace_size doesn't work Environment TensorRT Version: 8.2.1.8 NVIDIA GPU: V100 NVIDIA Driver Version: 470.82.01 CUDA Version: 11.4 CUDNN Version: 8.2 Operating System: linux Python Version: 3.8.8 PyTorch Version: 1.10.1 Steps To Reproduce import time import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np import random  import tensorrt as trt from pytorch_quantization import nn as quant_nn from pytorch_quantization import calib from pytorch_quantization.tensor_quant import QuantDescriptor from pytorch_quantization import quant_modules  seed = 1234 np.random.seed(seed) random.seed(seed) torch.manual_seed(seed) torch.cuda.manual_seed(seed)  quant_modules.initialize()  quant_desc_input = QuantDescriptor(calib_method='max') quant_nn.QuantConv1d.set_default_quant_desc_input(quant_desc_input) quant_nn.TensorQuantizer.use_fb_fake_quant = True  class Net(torch.nn.Module):     def __init__(self):         super().__init__()          self.conv1 = torch.nn.Conv1d(256, 256, 3, padding=243, dilation=243, bias=False)         self.act = torch.nn.LeakyReLU(negative_slope=0.2)      def forward(self, x):         out = self.conv1(x)         out = self.act(out)         return out   def collect_stats(model, data, num_batches):     """Feed data to the network and collect statistic"""      # Enable calibrators     for name, module in model.named_modules():         if isinstance(module, quant_nn.TensorQuantizer):             if module._calibrator is not None:                 module.disable_quant()                 module.enable_calib()             else:                 module.disable()      model(data)      # Disable calibrators     for name, module in model.named_modules():         if isinstance(module, quant_nn.TensorQuantizer):             if module._calibrator is not None:                 module.enable_quant()                 module.disable_calib()             else:                 module.enable()  def compute_amax(model, **kwargs):     # Load calib result     for name, module in model.named_modules():         if isinstance(module, quant_nn.TensorQuantizer):             if module._disabled:                 continue             if module._calibrator is not None:                 if isinstance(module._calibrator, calib.MaxCalibrator):                     module.load_calib_amax()                 else:                     module.load_calib_amax(**kwargs)             print(F"{name:40}: {module}") #    model.cuda()   def onnx_to_tensorrt(onnx_model_path, trt_model_path):     trt_logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.VERBOSE)     trt_builder = trt.Builder(trt_logger)     trt_builder.max_batch_size = 1     explicit_batch = 1 << int(trt.NetworkDefinitionCreationFlag.EXPLICIT_BATCH)     trt_network = trt_builder.create_network(explicit_batch)     trt_parser = trt.OnnxParser(trt_network, trt_logger)     with open(onnx_model_path, "rb") as f:         assert trt_parser.parse(f.read())     trt_config = trt_builder.create_builder_config()     trt_config.max_workspace_size = (1 << 30)     trt_config.flags |= 1 << int(trt.BuilderFlag.INT8)     trt_engine = trt_builder.build_engine(trt_network, trt_config)     with open(trt_model_path, "wb") as f:         f.write(trt_engine.serialize())  def run_tensorrt(trt_model_path, input_array):     trt_logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)     trt_runtime = trt.Runtime(trt_logger)     with open(trt_model_path, "rb") as f:         trt_engine = trt_runtime.deserialize_cuda_engine(f.read())     trt_context = trt_engine.create_execution_context()     trt_input = torch.tensor(input_array, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")     trt_output = torch.empty(tuple(trt_engine.get_binding_shape(1)), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")     bindings = [trt_input.data_ptr(), trt_output.data_ptr()]     trt_context.execute_v2(bindings=bindings)     return trt_output.cpu().numpy()  if __name__ == "__main__":     # define model     model = Net()     model.eval()      print(model)      data = torch.tensor(np.random.rand(1, 256, 1000).astype(np.float32))     with torch.no_grad():         collect_stats(model, data, num_batches=1)         compute_amax(model, method="percentile", percentile=100)      input_array = np.random.rand(1, 256, 1000).astype(np.float32)     dummy_input = torch.tensor(input_array)      torch.onnx.export(         model, dummy_input, "/tmp/test.onnx", verbose=True, opset_version=13)      # onnx to tensorrt     onnx_to_tensorrt(onnx_model_path="/tmp/test.onnx", trt_model_path="/tmp/engine.bin")      # tensorrt inference     trt_out = run_tensorrt(trt_model_path="/tmp/engine.bin", input_array=input_array)     # pytorch inference, qdq     pytorch_out = model(dummy_input)      print("TRT out", trt_out.shape, trt_out)     print("pytorch out", pytorch_out.shape, pytorch_out)

Environment TensorRT Version: 8.2.3.0 NVIDIA GPU: GeForce GTX 1080 ti NVIDIA Driver Version: 460.91.03 CUDA Version: CUDNN Version: Operating System: Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS Python Version (if applicable): 3.6 Tensorflow Version (if applicable): PyTorch Version (if applicable): 1.8 Baremetal or Container (if so, version): Relevant Files The onnx model that cause troubles. threshold.zip Steps To Reproduce The script I use to reproduce the error : import torch import tensorrt as trt  TRT_LOGGER = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING) trt_runtime = trt.Runtime(TRT_LOGGER)   def tensorrt_export(onnx_path, input_values):     with trt.Builder(TRT_LOGGER) as builder, builder.create_network(         1     ) as network, builder.create_builder_config() as config, trt.OnnxParser(         network, TRT_LOGGER     ) as parser:         config.max_workspace_size = 256 << 20         with open(onnx_path, "rb") as model:             parser.parse(model.read())             network.get_input(0).shape = input_values.shape         engine = builder.build_engine(network, config)          assert engine is not None   class Model(torch.nn.Module):     def forward(self, x):         mask = (x > 0.).float()  # ko         return mask   if __name__ == "__main__":     ONNX_PATH = "/tmp/threshold.onnx"     model = Model()     input_x = torch.rand(1, 32)      # torch inference     model(input_x)      # generate the ONNX model (the result has been posted in the "Relevant Files" section of this issue     torch.onnx.export(         model,         input_x,         ONNX_PATH,         verbose=True,         input_names=["x"],         output_names=["output"],         opset_version=11,     )      # convert to TRT     tensorrt_export(ONNX_PATH, input_x)  This script runs correctly with trt v7 but fails with trt v8. title: TensorRT quits Python if TensorFlow is imported
author: daniel-kukiela
body: Description TensorRT code silently quits Python if TensorFlow is imported. Environment TensorRT Version: 8.2.3.0 NVIDIA GPU: GTX 1080Ti / RTX 8000 NVIDIA Driver Version: 30.0.15.1123 CUDA Version: 11.4.3 CUDNN Version: 8.2.4.15 Operating System: Windows 10 21H2 Python Version (if applicable): 3.9.6 Tensorflow Version (if applicable): 2.7.0 (tested also with 2.5.0) Baremetal or Container (if so, version): baremetal Relevant Files Used plan file: https://www.dropbox.com/s/mbsnwesfb0wmbp3/upsample_fp16.plan?dl=0 Steps To Reproduce import tensorrt as trt import pycuda.driver as cuda import pycuda.autoinit import tensorflow   file = 'upsample_fp16.plan' f = open(file, 'rb')  TRT_LOGGER = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING) trt_runtime = trt.Runtime(TRT_LOGGER) engine = trt_runtime.deserialize_cuda_engine(f.read()) print(engine.get_binding_shape(0)) print(set(engine.get_binding_shape(0))) print(trt.volume(engine.get_binding_shape(0))) If you comment out import tensorflow the code works, otherwise silently quits Python.

title: [myelin][onnx] Assertion failuers on logical operator (seems buffer overwritten by downstream node?)
author: lazycal
body: Description Either logical_op followed by reshape or reshape followed by logical_op may trigger an error. They look similar so I'm filing in the same issue. See my next comment. It looks like it's because logical operators are not operating on the right tensor buffer; or their buffers are overwritten by downstream nodes. logical_op->reshape When a boolean tensor is reshaped and the target shape happens to be the same, any further operations (even identity_op) on the before-reshape tensor will trigger assertion failures [TensorRT] ERROR: 2: [myelinCopyLayer.cpp::addCopy::14] Error Code 2: Internal Error (Assertion node.params.origin == CopyOrigin::kIDENTITY failed.). Below is the minimal reproducible onnx model: import numpy as np import torch  inputs = {     'i3': np.random.rand(2, 48).astype(np.float32), }   class Model(torch.nn.Module):     def __init__(self) -> None:         super().__init__()      @torch.no_grad()     def forward(self, i3):         g = i3 > 0         a = g.reshape(2, 48)         # a = g.reshape(1, 48 * 2) # this would be fine however          # any of the following crashes TensorRT         b = g         # b = torch.all(g)         # b = g.to(torch.int32)         # b = torch.sum(g)          # but fine with any of the following         # b = torch.all(a)         # b = a.to(torch.int32)         # b = torch.sum(a)         return (a, b)   model = Model() model.eval() torch_inp = {k: torch.from_numpy(v) for k, v in inputs.items()} torch.onnx.export(     model, tuple(torch_inp.values()),     "output.onnx", input_names=list(inputs.keys()),     verbose=False, opset_version=14)  My best guess is that the Reshape op is getting optimized to an no-op, but that somehow changed the tensor buffer in place, but the logical op still needs the original buffer. reshape->logical_op Interestingly, in a slightly different model with their order switched, it still triggers an error, though different: python: /root/gpgpu/MachineLearning/myelin/src/compiler/.././compiler/kernel_gen/cuda_codegen/cuda_codegen.hpp:285: const string& myelin::kgen::cuda_codegen_t::crd_t::operator[](size_t) const: Assertion `i < crds_.size()' failed. Below are the model and the code import numpy as np import torch  inputs = {     'i3': np.random.rand(1, 3, 48, 48).astype(np.float32), }   class Model(torch.nn.Module):     def __init__(self) -> None:         super().__init__()      @torch.no_grad()     def forward(self, i3):         r = i3.reshape(4, 1, 1728, 1)         a = torch.sqrt(r)  # other ops seem fine         a = torch.squeeze(a, 1)         g = r > 0         # any of the following crashes TensorRT         b = g         # b = torch.all(g)         # b = g.to(torch.int32)         # b = torch.sum(g)         return (a, b)   model = Model() model.eval() torch_inp = {k: torch.from_numpy(v) for k, v in inputs.items()} torch.onnx.export(     model, tuple(torch_inp.values()),     "output.onnx", input_names=list(inputs.keys()),     output_names=['o0'],     verbose=False, opset_version=14)  This one is more criptic. I don't have any guess for it. title: Myelin error on onnx model: Assertion `i < crds_.size()' failed
author: lazycal
body: Description I got different result than PyTorch or a crash with error trtexec: /root/gpgpu/MachineLearning/myelin/src/compiler/.././compiler/kernel_gen/cuda_codegen/cuda_codegen.hpp:322: const string& myelin::kgen::cuda_codegen_t::crd_t::operator[](size_t) const: Assertion `i < crds_.size()' failed. when running on an onnx model that does reshape->sqrt->squeeze. The minimal reproducible model: import numpy as np import torch  inputs = {     'i3': np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=(20, 20, 1)).astype(np.float32),     # 'i3': np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=(1, 20, 20, 1)).astype(np.float32), # incorrect result }   class Model(torch.nn.Module):     def __init__(self) -> None:         super().__init__()      @torch.no_grad()     def forward(self, i3):         r = i3.reshape(20 * 20, 1, 1)         # r = i3.reshape(1, 20 * 20, 1, 1) # incorrect result         a0 = torch.sqrt(r)         a = torch.squeeze(a0, -1)         g = r > 0         return (a, g)   model = Model() model.eval() torch_inp = {k: torch.from_numpy(v) for k, v in inputs.items()} torch.onnx.export(     model, tuple(torch_inp.values()),     "output.onnx", input_names=list(inputs.keys()),     verbose=False, opset_version=14) import onnx import onnx.checker  onnx_model = onnx.load("output.onnx") onnx.checker.check_model(onnx_model)  If use those two commented-out lines to replace their previous line, I got different result compared to PyTorch. And I tried removing any of those 4 ops, and that will make this error disappear. body: Description Attempting to load an ONNX model with the TensorRT execution provider on the NVidia TensorRT docker image (from AWS marketplace, hosted on the NVidia Deep Learning AMI also from AWS marketplace) fails with: RuntimeError: /onnxruntime_src/onnxruntime/core/providers/cuda/cuda_call.cc:122 bool onnxruntime::CudaCall(ERRTYPE, const char*, const char*, ERRTYPE, const char*) [with ERRTYPE = cudaError; bool THRW = true] /onnxruntime_src/onnxruntime/core/providers/cuda/cuda_call.cc:116 bool onnxruntime::CudaCall(ERRTYPE, const char*, const char*, ERRTYPE, const char*) [with ERRTYPE = cudaError; bool THRW = true] CUDA failure 35: CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version ; GPU=0 ; hostname=8f2a5528ea84 ; expr=cudaSetDevice(device_id_);  Environment TensorRT Version: 8.2.2 NVIDIA GPU: V100 NVIDIA Driver Version: 460.73.01 CUDA Version: 11.6 CUDNN Version: 8.3.2 Operating System: Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS Python Version (if applicable): 3.8.10 Tensorflow Version (if applicable): N/A PyTorch Version (if applicable): N/A Baremetal or Container (if so, version): NVidia TensorRT 22.01 (https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-jbbleexnwpstk) Relevant Files Minimal ONNX model created on a CPU installation of pytorch using the script: import torch import argparse   class MinimalModel(torch.nn.Module):     def __init__(self):         super(MinimalModel, self).__init__()         self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(5, 2)      def forward(self, x):         return self.linear(x)   if __name__ == "__main__":     # Parse arguments     parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()     parser.add_argument('--file', type=str, help='Path to save ONNX model to')     parser.add_argument('--dummy')     args = parser.parse_args()      model = MinimalModel()      # Export to ONNX     x = torch.randn(5)     # traced_script_module = torch.jit.trace(self.model, waveform, strict=False, check_trace=True)     torch.onnx.export(model,                     # model being run                       x,                         # model input (or a tuple for multiple inputs)                       args.file,                 # where to save the model (can be a file or file-like object)                       export_params=True,        # store the trained parameter weights inside the model file                       opset_version=11,          # the ONNX version to export the model to                       do_constant_folding=True,  # whether to execute constant folding for optimization                       input_names = ['input'],   # the model's input names                       output_names = ['output']  # the model's output names                       )  Minimal test loader (that is run on the tensorRT environment as detailed below): import os import argparse import onnxruntime   def run(onnx):     if not os.path.exists(onnx):         raise ValueError("Specified model file not found")      #  'TensorrtExecutionProvider',     ort_session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession(onnx,                                                providers=['TensorrtExecutionProvider'])     print(f"ONNX device: {onnxruntime.get_device()}")     print(f"Session providers: {ort_session.get_providers()}")   if __name__ == "__main__":     # Parse arguments     parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()     parser.add_argument('--onnx', type=str, help='Optional path to save/restore ONNX to and run with ONNX runtime')     parser.add_argument('--dummy')     args = parser.parse_args()      run(args.onnx)  Steps To Reproduce   Build minimal ONNX model (see script above) to serve as test model (any ONNX model should do really).  I did this on my Mac locally and then copied it to a mounted volume on the test VM.  The env that built this should not be terribly relevant, but I kept it separate from the tensorRT VM so as not to have to install pytorch there.  For ref it was python 3.7.10 with torch 1.1   Shell into TensorRT docker container.  The setup for this was an EC2 VM running he NVidia Deep Learning AMI (https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-e7zxdqduz4cbs?qid=1606075638508&sr=0-1&ref_=srh_res_product_title#pdp-overview), hosting docker with the container being the NVidia TensorRT container image from the AWS marketplace (https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-jbbleexnwpstk):   docker run -it -v /ebs:/ebs 709825985650.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/nvidia/containers/nvidia/tensorrt:22.01-py3 bash  Here 709825985650.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/nvidia/containers/nvidia/tensorrt:22.01-py3 is just my local copy of the TensorRT base image (no modifications) and /ebs is just an external mount containing the test runtime script (above) and the test model image (as generated by the script above)  Install the ONNX runtime (ephemerally for the sake of a minimally intrusive test that doesn't require me to build a bespoke container on top of the base TensorRT image):  pip install onnxruntime-gpu   Attempt to run the minimal loader script :  python onnx_load_test.py /ebs/models/minimal_model.onnx  Result is a runtime-driver mismatch error being reported: Traceback (most recent call last):   File "onnx_load_test.py", line 37, in <module>     run(args.onnx)   File "onnx_load_test.py", line 14, in run     ort_session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession(onnx,   File "/usr/local/lib/python3.8/dist-packages/onnxruntime/capi/onnxruntime_inference_collection.py", line 335, in __init__     self._create_inference_session(providers, provider_options, disabled_optimizers)   File "/usr/local/lib/python3.8/dist-packages/onnxruntime/capi/onnxruntime_inference_collection.py", line 379, in _create_inference_session     sess.initialize_session(providers, provider_options, disabled_optimizers) RuntimeError: /onnxruntime_src/onnxruntime/core/providers/cuda/cuda_call.cc:122 bool onnxruntime::CudaCall(ERRTYPE, const char*, const char*, ERRTYPE, const char*) [with ERRTYPE = cudaError; bool THRW = true] /onnxruntime_src/onnxruntime/core/providers/cuda/cuda_call.cc:116 bool onnxruntime::CudaCall(ERRTYPE, const char*, const char*, ERRTYPE, const char*) [with ERRTYPE = cudaError; bool THRW = true] CUDA failure 35: CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version ; GPU=0 ; hostname=21b052b97708 ; expr=cudaSetDevice(device_id_);  Since its driver version 460.73.01 and CUDA 11.6, which requires driver >=450.80.02 this seems like it should not occur...

title: Failing to load ONNX model
author: Bidski

However, my loading code which is, as far as I can tell, identical to the trtexec code is failing to build the ICudaEngine. title: `BatchedNMSPlugin::getOutputDimensions()` reports wrong `num_detections` shape
author: maminus
body: Description In the specification, num_detections has shape of [batch_size, 1]. But BatchedNMSPlugin::getOutputDimensions() reports shape of [batch_size]. The following is diff of trtexec log.(actual vs expected) -[V] [TRT] node_of_num_detections [BatchedNMS_TRT] outputs: [num_detections -> (16)[INT32]], [nmsed_boxes -> (16, 50, 4)[FLOAT]], [nmsed_scores -> (16, 50)[FLOAT]], [nmsed_classes -> (16, 50)[FLOAT]],  +[V] [TRT] node_of_num_detections [BatchedNMS_TRT] outputs: [num_detections -> (16, 1)[INT32]], [nmsed_boxes -> (16, 50, 4)[FLOAT]], [nmsed_scores -> (16, 50)[FLOAT]], [nmsed_classes -> (16, 50)[FLOAT]],  now batch_size=16, keepTopK=50. So num_detections expected shape of (16, 1), but actually shape of (16). It seems BatchedNMSPlugin::getOutputDimensions() expects following code.          // num_detections          if (index == 0)          {              Dims dim0{}; -            dim0.nbDims = 0; +            dim0.nbDims = 1; +            dim0.d[0] = 1;              return dim0;          } Environment TensorRT Version: 8.0.1 NVIDIA GPU: Jetson AGX Xavier Developer Kit NVIDIA Driver Version: N/A CUDA Version: 10.2 CUDNN Version: 8.2.1 Operating System: L4T 32.6.1 Python Version (if applicable): 3.6.9 Tensorflow Version (if applicable): 2.6.2+nv21.12 PyTorch Version (if applicable): 1.8.1 Baremetal or Container (if so, version): Container l4t-base r32.6.1 Relevant Files no external links because all necessary scripts and logs are showed at next section(Steps To Reproduce). Steps To Reproduce  run following python script to generate minimal reproducable ONNX file.  # generate minimal_nms.onnx in current directory. $ python3 generate_minimal_reproduce_model.py  generate_minimal_reproduce_model.py import onnx import onnx.numpy_helper import numpy as np   inputs = [     onnx.helper.make_tensor_value_info('boxes', onnx.TensorProto.FLOAT, [16, 100, 1, 4]),     onnx.helper.make_tensor_value_info('scores', onnx.TensorProto.FLOAT, [16, 100, 20]), ] outputs = [     onnx.helper.make_tensor_value_info('result_detections', onnx.TensorProto.INT64, [16, 1]) ] # BatchedNMS_TRT -> Add nodes = [     onnx.helper.make_node('BatchedNMS_TRT',         ['boxes', 'scores'],         ['num_detections', 'nmsed_boxes', 'nmsed_scores', 'nmsed_classes'],         shareLocation=1,         backgroundLabelId=-1,         numClasses=20,         topK=100,         keepTopK=50,         scoreThreshold=0.5,         iouThreshold=0.9,         isNormalized=0,         clipBoxes=0,         domain='tensorrt'),     # expected shape is Add([16, 1], [16, 1]) -> [16, 1]     onnx.helper.make_node('Add', ['num_detections', 'dummy_coeff'], ['result_detections']), ] inits = [     onnx.numpy_helper.from_array(np.zeros([16, 1], dtype=np.int64), 'dummy_coeff'), ] opsets = [     onnx.helper.make_opsetid('', 11),     onnx.helper.make_opsetid('tensorrt', 11), ] model = onnx.helper.make_model(onnx.helper.make_graph(nodes, 'minimal_nms', inputs, outputs, inits), opset_imports=opsets, ir_version=7) onnx.checker.check_model(model) onnx.save(model, 'minimal_nms.onnx') title: platforms vs. GPU architectures vs. GPU one specific model
author: leimeng86
body: For Q1, there is no guarantee the serialized engine will work on different platforms, as the optimized graph uses kernels specific to the GPU.  If you are running on different machines with the Same GPU architecture/OS it should work. You can support multiple GPU's as backends, with multiple saved serialized engines with TRT-IS (Inference Server) if you are trying to support a larger collection of GPU's as one suggestion. title: pytorch-quantization example classfication_flow.py has incorrect import path
author: Jeremalloch
body: In the tools/pytorch-quantization/examples/torchvision/classification_flow.py file, in line 42, custom (Nvidia modified) pytorch models are imported.  However, the code defining these models was later nested further under a classification directory, so the correct path should be models.classification.  In the same file, a check is performed to see if a custom implementation exists for a model (specified by name), or if the script should fall back to torchvision implementation.  This incorrect path results in the model always falling back to the torchvision implementation, without warning to the user.  The modified models were authored because they made minor changes to allow quantization of residual connections (during TRT export), but by falling back to the torchvision implementation, the residual connections are left unquantized, resulting in a slower model. The first figure below is a Netron visualization of a block in a ResNet-50 onnx model generated by the current implementation of the classification_flow.py script.  The second figure, below, highlights the addition of the QuantizeLinear and DequantizeLinear layers along the residual path that are added by the custom implementation:  Environment N/A, this is a universal issue. Relevant Files In this Google drive folder, I have included the above screenshots, as well as the onnx files that were used to generate them. Steps To Reproduce Run the Nvidia authored classification_flow.py already included in the repository.  Then either insert a PDB breakpoint at line 150 to verify this path is never being reached, or visualize the exported onnx file and verify the lack of QuantizeLinear and DequantizeLinear layers along residual paths.

title: Question about fast model loading time
author: AsiaCao
body: Description Hi team, I just have a question to confirm. Please let me know if there is a better forum for such questions. I did some preliminary benchmark in Python TensorRT APIs to see how fast it is to load a model into memory and make an inference. I noticed that it took about 8 seconds to load a model into memory and make an inference. After that, if i load a different model into memory and make a single inference, it's really fast (as long as it's still the same python process/session). The entire process of loading a model and making one inference only took less than 0.5s, even the model is completely different. I was wondering is this behavior normal or expected? if so, what happened internally that makes the subsequent load-and-inference so fast, even it's a different model? and also curious why the first load-and-inference takes 8 seconds. The benchmark was set up as follows:  prepared 4 compiled TensorRT models (engine files). they are object detection models with different architectures. each model is around 100MB. i copied each model 50 times on disk, each one has a different name. now i have a model pool of 200 models. then i ran the following operations repeatedly and measure the time: a. randomly pick an image b. randomly pick a model on disk c. load the the selected model into memory d. make a prediction and print the result  E.g. a+b+c+d took a total of 8s in the first time, then the subsequent a+b+c+d only took around 0.5 second consistently. title: [Bug] crash on poolings with larger-than-317 pool sizes
author: ganler
body: Description A simple pooling 2d (can be AvgPool/MaxPool etc.) layer whose sizes are greater or equal to 317 will lead to TRT crash. This can be fixed on user side by using multiple smaller poolings but just want report this case to improve TRT's robustness. :-) I am new here so I just randomly cc some active developers: @nvpohanh @zerollzeng @ttyio Environment TensorRT Version:  8.4.1.5 NVIDIA GPU:  3080Ti NVIDIA Driver Version: 510.73.08 CUDA Version: 11.6 CUDNN Version: 8.4.1 Operating System: Ubuntu 20.04 Python Version (if applicable): 3.8 PyTorch Version (if applicable): 1.13.0.dev20220624+cu113 Relevant Files The ONNX model can be generated by script below. Steps To Reproduce # Build network and export to ONNX 14 import torch  ksize = (317, 317)  class Net(torch.nn.Module):     def __init__(self):         super(Net, self).__init__()         self.pool = torch.nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=ksize)      def forward(self, x):         return self.pool(x)   x = torch.rand((1, 3, *ksize), dtype=torch.float32) torch.onnx.export(Net().eval(), x, "output.onnx", opset_version=14)  # Check if the model is strictly valid import onnx onnx_model = onnx.load("output.onnx") model = onnx.checker.check_model(onnx_model, full_check=True)  # Compile with TensorRT but get crashed. import tensorrt as trt builder = trt.Builder(trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)) network = builder.create_network(1 << (int)(     trt.NetworkDefinitionCreationFlag.EXPLICIT_BATCH)) config = builder.create_builder_config() config.set_memory_pool_limit(trt.MemoryPoolType.WORKSPACE, 1 * 1 << 30) parser = trt.OnnxParser(network, trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)) assert parser.parse(onnx._serialize(onnx_model)) builder.build_engine(network, config) Errors: """ [06/25/2022-18:56:24] [TRT] [E] [network.cpp::addPoolingNd::1025] Error Code 3: API Usage Error (Parameter check failed at: optimizer/api/network.cpp::addPoolingNd::1025, condition: allDimsGtEq(windowSize, 1) && volume(windowSize) < MAX_KERNEL_DIMS_PRODUCT(nbSpatialDims) ) [1]    930974 segmentation fault (core dumped)  ipython """

title: [Feature request] Make using incompatible timing caches for building CUDA engines not a hard error
author: dev0x13
body: Description I am currently researching ways for speeding up building TensorRT's CUDA engines in the runtime from ONNX models using the C++ API. That is, I am loading the ONNX file, building a CUDA engine from it and then using the latter for inference. For some specific reasons it is not possible for my application neither to prebuild engines before running the application nor to store those on a filesystem for a future usage. Thus, I am looking for ways to improve CUDA engine building speed. I have explored all the available API options, and this exploration resulted in the Timing Cache being the best option for me. Here is the rough explanation of the approach I came up with:  Obtain several Timing Caches using several GPUs of architectures / CCs I want my application to support. Combine those caches into a single one. Provide the combined cache to a builder while building a CUDA engine from the ONNX file. Build the CUDA engine fast, because the provided Timing Cache already contains needed profiling metrics.  Unfortunately, the last step fails in some specific environments with the following error message: [TensorRT] 2: [caskBuilderUtils.cpp::getCaskHandle::408] Error Code 2: Internal Error (Assertion !isGroupConv || (findConvShaderByHandle(klib, caskHandle) || cask_trt::availableLinkableConvShaders()->findByHandle(caskHandle)) failed. ) [TensorRT] 2: [builder.cpp::buildSerializedNetwork::636] Error Code 2: Internal Error (Assertion engine != nullptr failed. )  I suspect that the builder is picking some tactic from the provided cache, but the tactic is not available on the current GPU device. Assuming this guess is right, it does not seem to be an inevitable error since the incompatible tactic could be skipped (I tried setting the ignoreMismatch flag with no luck). So the feature request is essentially to make the build skip the cache entry and proceed instead of throwing a hard error. P.S. I am aware that timing cache is not recommended to be reused across devices, but my benchmarks shows that it's harmless. title: Built engine failed to include optimization profile with dynamic input shapes
author: nguyenvanhoang7398
body: I'm trying to build an engine from an Onnx network which inputs are of dynamic shapes. After creating an optimization profile and specifying the min, opt, and max shapes the built engine doesn't incorporate this profile. Below is the code to reproduce. from pathlib import Path import tensorrt as trt from translate.quantization.tensorrt import common    _folder = Path.cwd() saved_models_path = _folder.joinpath("tensorrt_models") TRT_LOGGER = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.VERBOSE)   def build_and_save_engine(onnx_file_path):     builder = trt.Builder(TRT_LOGGER)     network = builder.create_network(common.EXPLICIT_BATCH)     parser = trt.OnnxParser(network, TRT_LOGGER)     config = builder.create_builder_config()     profile = builder.create_optimization_profile()     with open(onnx_file_path, 'rb') as model:         if not parser.parse(model.read()):             print("ERROR: Failed to parse the ONNX file.")             for error in range(parser.num_errors):                 print(parser.get_error(error))             return None         print('Completed parsing of ONNX file')      print('Beginning ONNX file parsing')     print("Network inputs:")     for i in range(network.num_inputs):         tensor = network.get_input(i)         print(tensor.name, trt.nptype(tensor.dtype), tensor.shape)     # allow TensorRT to use up to 16GB of GPU memory for tactic selection     config.max_workspace_size = common.GiB(16)     builder.max_batch_size = 1      # set optimization profile for dynamic shape     min_length, max_length = 1, 200     opt_length = int(max_length / 2)     min_batch_size, max_batch_size = 1, 16     num_beams = 1     dim = 1024      profile.set_shape('input_ids', (min_batch_size * num_beams, 1),                       (min_batch_size * num_beams, 1),                       (min_batch_size * num_beams, 1))     profile.set_shape('encoder_attention_mask', (min_batch_size * num_beams, min_length),                       (min_batch_size * num_beams, opt_length),                       (min_batch_size * num_beams, max_length))     profile.set_shape('encoder_hidden_states', (min_batch_size * num_beams, min_length, dim),                       (min_batch_size * num_beams, opt_length, dim),                       (min_batch_size * num_beams, max_length, dim))      config.add_optimization_profile(profile)      engine = builder.build_engine(network, config)     context = engine.create_execution_context()     print(context.get_binding_shape(0))     print(context.get_binding_shape(1))     print(context.get_binding_shape(2))   if __name__ == "__main__":     build_and_save_engine("m2m100_418M-init-decoder.onnx")  It supposed to print the shapes of 3 inputs as (1, -1) (1, -1) (1, -1, 1024)  since the second dimension is dynamic but it prints (1, 1) (1, 1) (1, 1, 1024)  instead. Here is the Onnx model link. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1GU9DvZAo_G4MVpZ1i4pd7MFypP6OIFT_/view?usp=sharing Can someone please check if there's any problem with my implementation or if it's indeed a bug? Thank you. My environment: TensorRT: 8.4.1.6 Pytorch: 1.11.0 Onnx: 1.9.0 Cuda: 11.3

title: Not possible to declare pytorch-quantization as a dependency
author: pommedeterresautee
body: Description Currently, the only compiled version is for python 3.8: https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/redist/pytorch-quantization/ Moreover, the setup.py imports Pytorch without try / catch. https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/blob/main/tools/pytorch-quantization/setup.py#L23 Therefore, it is impossible to declare this package as a dependency of another one:  on the compiled version the support is limited to an old version of Python (which is not by default on an updated Ubuntu for instance); if one try to declare it as a Git dependency, there is crash risk during compilation if Pytorch is not already installed (e.g. blank virtual env, docker, etc.).  The solution would be to offer pre-compiled version at least for recent Python version, so something like >= 3.8. title: Get wrong quantization result after setting TensorQuantizer.use_fb_fake_quant = True
author: Wang-Qk
body: Description  It is caused by a bug from pytorch, as shown in the issus  "torch.fake_quantize_per_tensor_affine will affect the results of the model if the input memory is not contiguous". It has been fixed in pytorch, but may confuse someone like me using low version pytorch (1.8.1). When using the tool pytorch-quantization, before exporting a torch model into onnx one, we need set TensorQuantizer.use_fb_fake_quant = True, so that torch.onnx.export can parser the quanizer successfully. However, it means that torch.fake_quantize_per_tensor_affine may be called (tensor_quantizer.py#310) and the bug may be triggered. Maybe we could fix the bug with checking if the input is contiguous before calling torch.fake_quantize_per_tensor_affine in TensorQuantizer. title: Expose additional ONNX protobuf model properties via nvonnxparser::IParser
author: magnusmaynard
body: When parsing an ONNX model to build a TRT network, it would be useful to expose the additional parameters from the ONNX protobuf. Currently only the graph is exposed. auto onnx_parser = unique_ptr<nvonnxparser::IParser>(nvonnxparser::createParser(*network, getLogger())); onnx_parser->parseFromFile(onnx_path.c_str(), static_cast<int>(nvinfer1::ILogger::Severity::kINFO)))  These additional properties include:  doc_string domain ir_version metadata_props model_version opset_import producer_name producer_version  Often the metadata_props contain important information describing how to execute/interpret the model, for example the class names and preprocessing steps. In python, reading these parameters from the ONNX is straight forward, but via C++ it’s much more involved, having the compile/include the ONNX repo and avoid issues with protobuf size limits. As the ONNX is already being parsed by TRT, it would be straight forward to expose these properties somewhere on this interface. I would create a PR for this myself, but I believe the code is closed source. Let me know if it’s not.

author: wangshangsam
body: Description I've been trying to enable sparse tensor core on A100 and RTX3090 for the BERT SQuAD inference. However, even when I can see in Netron that the Gemm's weight satisfy the 2:4 sparsity pattern,  and I set --sparsity=force, trtexec still shows that "Layers eligible for sparse math:" is empty. Example log from trtexec using the command provided in the Steps To Reproduce section: [08/23/2022-16:17:57] [I] [TRT] Detected 3 inputs and 2 output network tensors. Args:             inputs (Dict[str, torch.Tensor]): The input name and tensor pairs.          Return:             Dict[str, torch.Tensor]: The output name and tensor pairs.         """         bindings = [None] * (len(self._input_names) + len(self._output_names))          for input_name, input_tensor in inputs.items():             idx = self.engine.get_binding_index(input_name)              # All input tensors must be gpu variables             input_tensor = input_tensor.contiguous()             if input_tensor.dtype == torch.long:                 input_tensor = input_tensor.int()             self.context.set_binding_shape(idx, tuple(input_tensor.shape))             bindings[idx] = input_tensor.contiguous().data_ptr()          # create output tensors         outputs = {}         for output_name in self._output_names:             idx = self.engine.get_binding_index(output_name)             dtype = TORCH_DTYPE_MAP[self.engine.get_binding_dtype(idx)]             shape = tuple(self.context.get_binding_shape(idx))              output = torch.empty(size=shape, dtype=dtype, device='cuda')             outputs[output_name] = output             bindings[idx] = output.data_ptr()          self.context.execute_async_v2(bindings,                                       torch.cuda.current_stream().cuda_stream)          return outputs   class TestModel(torch.nn.Module):      def __init__(self) -> None:         super().__init__()      def forward(self, x):         batch_size = x.size(0)         C = x.size(1)         max_x, _ = x.max(-1)         _, inds = max_x.topk(4)         batch_inds = torch.arange(batch_size, device=inds.device).unsqueeze(-1)          # new_x = torch.gather(x, 1, inds.unsqueeze(-1).expand(batch_size, 4, 4))         new_x = x[batch_inds, inds, ...]         # new_x = x.flatten(0, 1)[inds + batch_inds * C]         return new_x, inds + batch_inds * C   def main():     # models     model = TestModel().cuda()     x = torch.rand(1, 10, 4).cuda()      # export onnx     input_names = ['input']     output_names = ['output', 'inds']     torch.onnx.export(         model,         x,         'tmp.onnx',         input_names=input_names,         output_names=output_names,         dynamic_axes={'input': {             0: 'b',             1: 'n'         }},         opset_version=11)      # export tensorrt     input_shapes = {         'input': {             'min_shape': [1, 5, 4],             'opt_shape': [2, 10, 4],             'max_shape': [4, 40, 4]         }     }     engine = from_onnx(         'tmp.onnx', input_shapes=input_shapes, max_workspace_size=1 << 30)      wrapper = TRTWrapper(engine)      x = torch.rand(2, 10, 4).cuda()      torch_out = model(x)     out = wrapper({'input': x})     out = [out[name] for name in output_names]      # print(x)      for o, to in zip(out, torch_out):         print(o.shape)         torch.testing.assert_allclose(o, to)      # print(torch_out)   if __name__ == '__main__':     main()

title: How to quantize concat and element-wise operators (add, mul, etc.) by pytorch_quantization?
author: shuo-ouyang
body: Hi guys, I quantized all conv2d/transposeconv2d/gemm/maxpooling ops in my pytroch model using pytorch_quantization and obtained a well-performed int8 model. Now I want to quantize concat and element-wise ops to improve inference performance, so is there any approach to implement quantized concat/add/mul, etc. in pytroch_quantization tools? Thank you~ It is noticed that the quantized modules are derived fromtorch.nn.module and _utils.QuantInputMixin, such as the following QuantMaxPool2d class. But concat/add/mul are not implemented as a module in pytorch, so I do not know how to quantize them... class QuantMaxPool2d(pooling.MaxPool2d, _utils.QuantInputMixin):     """Quantized 2D maxpool"""     def __init__(self, kernel_size, stride=None, padding=0, dilation=1,                  return_indices=False, ceil_mode=False, **kwargs):         super(QuantMaxPool2d, self).__init__(kernel_size, stride, padding, dilation,                                              return_indices, ceil_mode)         quant_desc_input = _utils.pop_quant_desc_in_kwargs(self.__class__, input_only=True, **kwargs)         self.init_quantizer(quant_desc_input)      def forward(self, input):         quant_input = self._input_quantizer(input)         return super(QuantMaxPool2d, self).forward(quant_input)

title: Performance of structured sparsity for Inceptionv3 on A6000 GPU
author: shivmgg
body: Hi, I trained and ran the dense and 2:4 structured sparse model for the InceptionV3 model on the NVIDIA A6000 GPU. However, I observe marginal performance improvement and even worse runtime with larger batch sizes. Here are the latency numbers (in ms) for various batch sizes.    Batch Size 32 64 128 256     Dense 10.4 19.83 37.94 74.73   2:4 structured model 9.97 19.08 36.69 91.86    I used the following model files for batch size 32: Dense Model: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1UtARXRPJZNs4_6Hsv9BcUmxP6V6GAaPn/view?usp=sharing Sparse Model: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Czbgt7yV_LfBmtlU7XvtF1by1Js0upwZ/view?usp=sharing I used the following command to run the model with TensorRT: trtexec --onnx=inception_sparse_model.onnx --fp16 --saveEngine=inception_pytorch_sparse.trt --sparsity=enable --explicitBatch --workspace=40000 Please let me know if the performance can be improved.

So I should expect a model which is at least 2x smaller in size and 2x faster for inference. However, my model size and inference speed are both same as FP32. I print out the model and can see that the Conv2d and Convtransposed2D are replaced by quant variants. Please help me understand this.  Environment TensorRT Version: NVIDIA GPU: RTX2080MaxQ NVIDIA Driver Version: 515.65 CUDA Version: 11.7 CUDNN Version: Operating System: Linux - NGC Tensorrt docker Python Version (if applicable): 3.8.10 Tensorflow Version (if applicable): PyTorch Version (if applicable): Baremetal or Container (if so, version): NGC Tensorrt Docker + Torch-Tensorrt installed from source Relevant Files  Steps To Reproduce  Here is part of the code I used to quantize. """ https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/blob/master/tools/pytorch-quantization/examples/calibrate_quant_resnet50.ipynb Quantizing followed by fine tune training """ import os, sys, socket import torch import torch.utils.data from torch import nn from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Dataset from pytorch_quantization import quant_modules from pytorch_quantization import nn as quant_nn from pytorch_quantization import calib from pytorch_quantization.tensor_quant import QuantDescriptor from settings import argo_settings as settings  # for argoverse from models import model_bevdetnet as model_simple import numpy as np from tqdm import tqdm import torchvision import timeit import matplotlib.pyplot as plt first create a dataset class CalibDataset(Dataset): """ Dataset class """ def __init__(self, path_calib_dataset_bev) -> None:     """     Default method     """      self.path_dataset_bev = path_calib_dataset_bev     frames = os.listdir(self.path_dataset_bev)  # returns a list of all file names in the passed directory path     print("Number of calib BEV images : ", len(frames))     self.framelist = frames  # save it to an object parameter     self.len = len(frames)  # this will be used by __len__()     np.random.shuffle(self.framelist)  # randomly shuffle all frames, no need to shuffle at test time     self.ERROR_LOGS_PRINT_ONCE = False  def __len__(self):     """     Returns the length of the dataset / number of frames     Returns: length of dataset     """      return self.len   def __getitem__(self, item):     """     Function does the actual data return to the calling iterator     Args:         item (): index of data item     Returns: the train_X, and other train_Ys     """      frame_path = self.path_dataset_bev + '/' + self.framelist[item]  # form comlplete file path for the indexed frame     file = np.load(frame_path)  # read in the npy file, 10 channels      # sanity check, if dataset not already in desired shape, crop from top     if file.shape != (settings.N_ROWS_RAW_BEV, settings.N_COLS_RAW_BEV, settings.N_CHANNELS_RAW_BEV):         if self.ERROR_LOGS_PRINT_ONCE is False:             print("WARNING : raw BEV shape : ", file.shape)             print("Cropping from top to {0} rows and {1} cols...".format(settings.N_ROWS_TRAIN_BEV, settings.N_COLS_TRAIN_BEV))          row_num_start = file.shape[0] - settings.N_ROWS_TRAIN_BEV         col_num_start = 0         col_num_end = settings.N_COLS_TRAIN_BEV          file = file[row_num_start:, col_num_start: col_num_end, :]                  if self.ERROR_LOGS_PRINT_ONCE is False:             print("Rehaped train frame -> ", file.shape)             self.ERROR_LOGS_PRINT_ONCE = True      # ------------------------------- NOTE: Since 31/07/22, channels order in BEV is ----------------------------------------#     # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 -> Z,D,I,X,Y, ring/laser_number     #------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------#      # extract all channels     ch_Z = file[:, :, 0]     ch_D = file[:, :, 1]     ch_I = file[:, :, 2]     ch_X = file[: ,:, 3]     ch_Y = file[:, :, 4]     ch_ring = file[:, :, 5]      if settings.ADD_BINARY_MASK is True:         train_x_normalized = np.zeros((settings.N_ROWS_TRAIN_BEV,                                          settings.N_COLS_TRAIN_BEV,                                          len(settings.TRAIN_BEV_CHANNEL_NAMES) + 1))     else:         train_x_normalized = np.zeros((settings.N_ROWS_TRAIN_BEV,                                          settings.N_COLS_TRAIN_BEV,                                          len(settings.TRAIN_BEV_CHANNEL_NAMES)))          for ch_index, train_feature_name in enumerate(settings.TRAIN_BEV_CHANNEL_NAMES):         if train_feature_name not in settings.channel_assignment_dict.keys():             print("ERROR: Selected BEV feature {0}, not found in {1}".format(train_feature_name, settings.channel_assignment_dict))             exit(-1)         else:             if train_feature_name == 'Z':                 train_x_normalized[:, :, ch_index] = ch_Z / 7.             if train_feature_name == 'D':                 train_x_normalized[:, :, ch_index] = ch_D / np.max(ch_D)             if train_feature_name == 'I':                     train_x_normalized[:, :, ch_index] = ch_I / np.max(ch_I)             if train_feature_name == 'X':                     train_x_normalized[:, :, ch_index] = ch_X / np.max(ch_X)             if train_feature_name == 'Y':                     train_x_normalized[:, :, ch_index] = ch_Y / np.max(ch_Y)             if train_feature_name == 'RING':                 train_x_normalized[:, :, ch_index] = ch_ring / 32          if settings.ADD_BINARY_MASK is True:         mask_r, mask_c = np.where(train_x_normalized[:, :, 0] != 0)  # get pixels that have value         train_x_normalized[mask_r, mask_c, -1] = 1.  # create binary mask          return torch.from_numpy(train_x_normalized).float().permute(2, 0, 1)  def collect_stats(model, data_loader, num_batches): """Feed data to the network and collect statistic""" # Enable calibrators for name, module in model.named_modules():     if isinstance(module, quant_nn.TensorQuantizer):         if module._calibrator is not None:             module.disable_quant()             module.enable_calib()         else:             module.disable()  # for i, (image, _) in tqdm(enumerate(data_loader), total=num_batches): #     model(image.cuda()) #     if i >= num_batches: #         break for i, image in tqdm(enumerate(data_loader), total=num_batches):     model(image.cuda())     if i >= num_batches:         break  # Disable calibrators for name, module in model.named_modules():     if isinstance(module, quant_nn.TensorQuantizer):         if module._calibrator is not None:             module.enable_quant()             module.disable_calib()         else:             module.enable()  def compute_amax(model, **kwargs): # Load calib result for name, module in model.named_modules(): if isinstance(module, quant_nn.TensorQuantizer): if module._calibrator is not None: if isinstance(module._calibrator, calib.MaxCalibrator): module.load_calib_amax() else: module.load_calib_amax(**kwargs) print(F"{name:40}: {module}") model.cuda()  def quantize_to_int8(fp32_pth_model_path, quantized_model_save_path): """ """ # set default quant descriptor quant_desc_input = QuantDescriptor(calib_method='histogram') quant_nn.QuantConv2d.set_default_quant_desc_input(quant_desc_input) quant_nn.QuantLinear.set_default_quant_desc_input(quant_desc_input) quant_nn.QuantConvTranspose2d.set_default_quant_desc_input(quant_desc_input) quant_nn.QuantAvgPool2d.set_default_quant_desc_input(quant_desc_input)  # init quantized modules quant_modules.initialize()  # load pretrained network network = model_simple.BevDetNetSimple(in_channels=settings.N_CHANNELS_TRAIN_BEV + 1,                                          out_kp_channels=settings.N_CHANNELS_PREDICTION_KP,                                          scale_H=2, scale_W=2, predict_3d_center=True).cuda() if fp32_pth_model_path is not None:     network.load_state_dict(torch.load(fp32_pth_model_path, map_location="cuda:0"))  # print(network)  # create data loader calib_dataset = CalibDataset(path_calib_dataset_bev=settings.WORKSPACE_ROOT_PATH + 'calib_data/') calib_loader = DataLoader(dataset=calib_dataset, batch_size=2, num_workers=1)  with torch.no_grad():     collect_stats(network, calib_loader, num_batches=6)     compute_amax(network, method="percentile", percentile=99.99)  torch.save(network.state_dict(), quantized_model_save_path)  def test_calibrated_inference(path_model_int8): """ runs inference with the int8 model on some test data """ quant_modules.initialize()  # trt_ts_module = torch.jit.load(path_model_int8).eval() network = model_simple.BevDetNetSimple(in_channels=settings.N_CHANNELS_TRAIN_BEV + 1,                                          out_kp_channels=settings.N_CHANNELS_PREDICTION_KP,                                          scale_H=2, scale_W=2, predict_3d_center=True).cuda() if path_model_int8 is not None:     network.load_state_dict(torch.load(path_model_int8, map_location="cuda:0"))  calib_dataset = CalibDataset(path_calib_dataset_bev=settings.WORKSPACE_ROOT_PATH + 'calib_data/') calib_loader = DataLoader(dataset=calib_dataset, batch_size=1, num_workers=1)  with torch.no_grad():     for i, data in enumerate(calib_loader):         bev_npy = data.permute(0, 2, 3, 1)[0].numpy()         bev = data.cuda()          t1 = timeit.default_timer()         kp, hwl, rot, dxdy = network(bev)         t2 = timeit.default_timer()         print("int8 inference ms --> ", (t2 - t1) * 1000)         kp_mask = torch.argmax(torch.softmax(kp, 1), 1).cpu().numpy()[0]         print(kp_mask.shape)          r, c = np.where(kp_mask == 1)         bev_npy[r, c, 0] = 1         image_path = settings.images_path + "anno_bev_int8_" + str(i) + '.png'         plt.imsave(image_path, bev_npy[:, :, 0:3])  if name == 'main': pth_model_path = settings.WORKSPACE_ROOT_PATH + 'trained_models/pth/argo_det_020922_zdirb_416x416_50mx2_e_80.pth' int8_model_path = settings.WORKSPACE_ROOT_PATH + 'trained_models/trt_ts/quant_model.pth' # quantize_to_int8(pth_model_path, int8_model_path)  test_calibrated_inference(int8_model_path)

title: feature request: support pytorch torchdynamo
author: Jack47
body: Torch-TensorRT acts as an extension to TorchScript.  But there are models that are not supported by pytorch jit tracing, see warning in jit tracing doc. Would you guys have plan to support torchDynamo to get torch.fx.GraphModule instead of jit.ScriptModule?  torchDynamo creates this FX Graph through bytecode analysis and is designed to mix Python execution with compiled backends to get the best of both worlds: usability and performance.

title: Dramatic performance difference running NeMo encoder comparing Tesla T4 and A100 accelerators
author: pks
body: Description While the performance of the encoder of NeMo's MTEncDec model is great on an A100 when using TensorRT, it is much less so on a Tesla T4 where TensorRT underperforms ONNXRUNTIME using the CUDAExecutionProvider. Encoding 1000 random inputs takes about 30 seconds with TensorRT on a T4, 5 seconds with TensorRT on an A100, and with ONNXRUNTIME on a T4 it's 25 seconds. I would expect TensorRT to outperform ONNXRUNTIME on a T4. Environment TensorRT Version: 8.4.2 NVIDIA GPU: A100-SXM4-40GB / Tesla T4 NVIDIA Driver Version: 470.82.01 (A100) / 515.65.01 (T4) CUDA Version: 11.7 CUDNN Version: 8.5.0 Operating System: CentOS Python Version (if applicable): 3.8.10 Tensorflow Version (if applicable): - PyTorch Version (if applicable): - Baremetal or Container (if so, version): container nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt:22.08-py3 Relevant Files A. Script to export encoder graph from NeMo: from nemo.collections.nlp.models import MTEncDecModel  model = MTEncDecModel.from_pretrained("nmt_en_de_transformer12x2") model.encoder.export("encoder.onnx")  B. ONNXRUNTIME test script: import numpy as np import onnxruntime import sys import time  sess_options = onnxruntime.SessionOptions() sess_options.graph_optimization_level = onnxruntime.GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT_ENABLE_ALL  providers = [     ('CUDAExecutionProvider', {         'device_id': 0,         'arena_extend_strategy': 'kNextPowerOfTwo',         'gpu_mem_limit': 2 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024,         'cudnn_conv_algo_search': 'EXHAUSTIVE',         'do_copy_in_default_stream': True,     }),     'CPUExecutionProvider', ]  encoder_session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession(sys.argv[1], providers=providers, sess_options=sess_options)  iters = 1000 max_len = 512 examples = [] for i in range(iters):     len_ = np.random.randint(1, 512)     examples.append((np.random.randint(30000, size=[1, len_], dtype=np.int64),                      np.ones([1, len_], dtype=np.int64))                    )  start = time.perf_counter() for i in range(iters):     encoder_input = {         "input_ids": examples[i][0],         "encoder_mask": examples[i][1],     }     encoder_output_names = ["last_hidden_states"]     _ = encoder_session.run(encoder_output_names, encoder_input)[0] total_time = time.perf_counter() - start print(f"{total_time}s")  C. Starting TensorRT's docker container for the following steps: nvidia-docker run --gpus all -it --rm nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt:22.08-py3  D. TensorRT conversion script: #!/usr/bin/env bash  trtexec \         --workspace=10000 \         --onnx=encoder.onnx  \         --saveEngine=encoder.trt-engine \         --minShapes=input_ids:1x1,encoder_mask:1x1 \         --maxShapes=input_ids:1x512,encoder_mask:1x512 \         --optShapes=input_ids:1x512,encoder_mask:1x512  E. TensorRT inference w/ polygraphy script: import numpy as np from polygraphy.backend.common import BytesFromPath from polygraphy.backend.trt import EngineFromBytes, TrtRunner import time  iters = 1000 max_len = 512 examples = [] for i in range(iters):     len_ = np.random.randint(1, max_len)     examples.append((np.random.randint(30000, size=[1, len_], dtype=np.int32),                      np.ones([1, len_], dtype=np.int32))                    )  load_engine = EngineFromBytes(BytesFromPath("encoder.trt-engine")) with TrtRunner(load_engine) as runner:     start = time.perf_counter()     for i in range(iters):         _ = runner.infer({"input_ids":examples[i][0],                           "encoder_mask":examples[i][1]})     end = time.perf_counter() total_time = end - start print(f"{total_time}s")  Steps To Reproduce  Export encoder.onnx using script A Run inference w/ ONNXRUNTIME using script B Start docker container using script C Convert encoder.onnx to TensorRT engine using script D Run inference w/ polygraphy using script E  Run steps 3-5 with either T4 or A100 GPUs. Observe performance differences.

title: Faster RCNN on TensorRT from TLT
author: codesian
body: Hi! We train a Faster Rcnn model with resnet18 backbone on TLT 3.0 container, train and evaluate test, inference works perfect with int8 calibration. Here TLT config: faster_rcnn_config.txt We export model to an .etlt file, we call our output tensor NMS -o option. After this we export model with TLT-converter tool on Jetson NX with calibration options and sizes. Seems ok. We are using Tensor RT on a c++ environment to make inference. Tensor input/outputs sizes are: 0 - input_image      · 0 - 3      · 0 - 1080      · 0 - 1920 1 - NMS      · 0 - 1      · 0 - 100      · 0 - 7 2 - NMS_1      · 0 - 1      · 0 - 1      · 0 - 1  At this time, detections seems to be less than on TLT container inference, we think that its problem of image preprocess before pass to the input tensor. We have a Opencv Mat as RGB source image (image). As result we have 20-30% detections in coparision with tlt tests. As you can see reverse RGB order to BGR, substract channel mean and divide by 1.0 as tlt documentation says on input_image_config parameter specification. float* hostDataBuffer = static_cast<float*>(buffers.getHostBuffer("input_image")); float pixelMean[3]{103.939,116.779, 123.68};  for (int i = 0, volImg = C * H * W; i < 1; ++i){      for (int c = 0; c < C; ++c){          for (unsigned j = 0, volChl = H * W; j < volChl; ++j){               hostDataBuffer[i * volImg + c * volChl + j] = float(((float(image.data[j * C + 2- c])) - pixelMean[c]))/1.0F;          }      } }  buffers.copyInputToDevice(); bool status{true}; status = context->execute(1, buffers.getDeviceBindings().data()); buffers.copyOutputToHost(); const float* nms = static_cast<const float*>(buffers.getHostBuffer("NMS")); for (int det_id = 0; det_id <100; det_id++){       float x1 =  nms[det_id * 7 + 3]; }  I know that there are more recent versions, TAO and Jetpacks. Documentation about Faster on TLT its poor and outdated, NMS tensors are only refences on documentation, and tensor RT samples not cover this. TensorRT Version: 4. title: IOptimizationProfile->setDimensions() the dimension value will be modified after call buildEngineWithConfig
author: amazingyyc
body: Hi tensorrt I try to load a onnx model with dynamic shape. Got a weird problem after load model. My step: 1: Load onnx model like below: std::unique_ptr<nvinfer1::IBuilder> builder{       nvinfer1::createInferBuilder(gLogger)}; uint32_t flag = 1U << static_cast<uint32_t>(                       nvinfer1::NetworkDefinitionCreationFlag::kEXPLICIT_BATCH);    std::unique_ptr<nvinfer1::INetworkDefinition> network{       builder->createNetworkV2(flag)};    std::unique_ptr<nvonnxparser::IParser> parser{       nvonnxparser::createParser(*network, gLogger)};  parser->parseFromFile(           model_config.onnx_model_path.c_str(),           static_cast<int32_t>(nvinfer1::ILogger::Severity::kWARNING) 2: Set all input's dimension first dim to be -1, make it to be dynamic. for (int32_t i = 0; i < net->getNbInputs(); ++i) {     nvinfer1::ITensor* tensor = net->getInput(i);      nvinfer1::Dims dims = tensor->getDimensions();     if (dims.nbDims > 0) {       dims.d[0] = -1;       tensor->setDimensions(dims);     }   } 3:Create a IOptimizationProfile and set all input's profile dimension(min_batch_size:1, opt_batch_size:1024, max_batch_size:1024): for (int32_t i = 0; i < net->getNbInputs(); ++i) {     nvinfer1::ITensor* tensor = net->getInput(i); title: How to handle multiprocessing
author: GiteZz
body: Description We are creating a real time application that uses a TensorRT engine for object detection. We've previously done these by simply iterating over the cameras and then executing inference for each frame. However, now we are scaling to 10+ cameras and this doesn't work anymore. We know that we can hit ~150fps (batch size 1) on our model when we have no wait time for sample input. However with these multiple cameras the input delay is rather significant such that the GPU is only used 20% as we are waiting on new frames constantly. Therefore, we wanted to do the frame retrieval, processing and GPU copy in a different process (python multiprocessing to avoid GIL problems). However, we are running into the problem about how we should use the TensorRT engine in this scenario. Using multiple contexts is no problem for us, but we don't know if it possible to share the engine (or a reference somehow) between the processes? Using a Queue with multiple producers (camera) and a single consumer (model) doesn't work as the python interprocess communication is too much of an overhead (slower then 100fps for full resolution). We expect the same with the Triton server as this uses network communication. Environment TensorRT Version: 8.4.3.1 NVIDIA GPU: RTX3090 NVIDIA Driver Version: 470.141.03 CUDA Version: 11.7 CUDNN Version: 8 Operating System: Ubuntu 20.04 Python Version (if applicable): 3.8 PyTorch Version (if applicable): 1.12 Baremetal or Container (if so, version): nvidia/cuda:11.7.1-cudnn8-devel-ubuntu20.04

title: Feature request: Discard tactic/configuration if output is invalid
author: nrakltx
body: Hello, As part of an attempt to boost inference of the T5 encoder model using TRT, I have come across some annoying behaviours in the engine building logic. In particular, when converting the T5 v1.1 to FP16, it becomes too unstable and starts returning NaNs due to division by sqrt of subnormally small numbers etc (This has been documented extensibly on PyTorch and HuggingFace models but has yet to be solved efficiently). It would be extremely helpful if TRT could skip/discard tactics which output NaNs, as it doesn't matter how fast something runs, if it returns invalid values it is completely worthless. This would have majorly helped me as I wouldn't have needed to wait an hour and a half for the engine to fully build only to discover it, like it's original PyTorch counterpart, returns invalid values. Thank in advance N

author: fxmarty
body: Description Running trtexec with --verbose, we can get some logs as: [12/30/2022-19:01:17] [V] [TRT] Layer: /transformer/Constant_7_output_0 + (Unnamed Layer* 236) [Shuffle] Host Persistent: 0 Device Persistent: 0 Scratch Memory: 0  or [12/30/2022-19:01:01] [V] [TRT] --------------- Timing Runner: {ForeignNode[(Unnamed Layer* 5216) [Shuffle].../lm_head/Add]} (Myelin)  I can find a reference to Shuffle here: https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/developer-guide/index.html#dla-lay-supp-rest ("Shuffle layer") and here: https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/developer-guide/index.html#fusion-types . I guess the most informative bit is : Each Shuffle layer consists of a transpose, a reshape, and a second transpose. I think still that it would be helpful to precise what this Unnamed Layer corresponds exactly in the ONNX graph. To be able to debug easily. Moreover, inspecting my ONNX graph, I could not find a succession Transpose --> Reshape --> Transpose, and yet these logs (Unnamed Layer* 5216) [Shuffle] are showing in trtexec --verbose multiple time! The doc is misleading in this regard. The first instance of Shuffle in the log is: [12/30/2022-19:00:56] [V] [TRT] Running: ConstShuffleFusion on onnx::MatMul_2824 [12/30/2022-19:00:56] [V] [TRT] ConstShuffleFusion: Fusing onnx::MatMul_2824 with (Unnamed Layer* 67) [Shuffle]  giving no info as to what the MatMul is fused with. title: One execution context per optimization profile with dynamic shapes results in broken output (no errors)
author: skirsten
body: Description When trying to use one ExecutionContext per optimization profile, after the first reuse e.g.  Create context 0, set profile 0 Use context 0 Create context 1, set profile 1 Use context 1 Use context 0 <- broken  the output is broken. See below for more info. Environment TensorRT Version: 8.5.3.1 NVIDIA GPU: RTX 3090 NVIDIA Driver Version: 520.61.07 CUDA Version: 11.8 CUDNN Version: 8.7.0.84 Operating System: Ubuntu 22.04 Python Version (if applicable): Tensorflow Version (if applicable): PyTorch Version (if applicable): Baremetal or Container (if so, version): Steps To Reproduce This simplified code showcases the problem. Its based off of the                TensorRT/tools/Polygraphy/polygraphy/backend/trt/runner.py                    Line 302       in       b0c259a                                                 def _infer_impl_v3(self, feed_dict, copy_outputs_to_host):                     and works basically the same, except that there is one context per optimization profile. This is recommended by the documentation and would allow me to remove the overhead of the optimization profile switching. def infer(self, profile_index, stream_handle):     if profile_index in self.contexts:         context = self.contexts[profile_index]     else:         context = self.engine.create_execution_context()          assert context.set_optimization_profile_async(             profile_index=profile_index,             stream_handle=stream_handle,         )          self.contexts[profile_index] = context      for idx in range(self.engine.num_io_tensors):         name = self.engine.get_tensor_name(idx)          assert not self.engine.is_shape_inference_io(             name         ), "shape inference is not supported"          assert (             self.engine.get_tensor_format(name) == trt.TensorFormat.LINEAR         ), "only linear tensors are supported"          mode = self.engine.get_tensor_mode(name)          if mode == trt.TensorIOMode.INPUT:             shape = ...              assert context.set_input_shape(name, shape)              tensor_ptr = ...              assert context.set_tensor_address(name, tensor_ptr)          elif mode == trt.TensorIOMode.OUTPUT:             shape = tuple(context.get_tensor_shape(name))              tensor_ptr = ...              assert context.set_tensor_address(name, tensor_ptr)          else:             raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected mode: {mode}")       assert context.execute_async_v3(stream_handle=stream_handle) engine.infer(0, stream_handle) engine.infer(1, stream_handle) engine.infer(0, stream_handle) # output is broken One thing to note is that the methods used should be the v3 variant (e.g. no profile specific names) yet I still get this warning: [TRT] [W] ICudaEngine::getProfileDimensions: bindingIndex 0 is not in profile 1. Using bindingIndex = 4 instead.  Considering I did not call getProfileDimensions I would guess that its called internally with the wrong index. Regardless that should not be the problem, just annoying, as the documentation states that this is automatically corrected. Replacing the start of the example with a single context if self.context:     context = self.context      if context.active_optimization_profile != profile_index:         assert context.set_optimization_profile_async(             profile_index=profile_index,             stream_handle=stream_handle,         )  else:     context = self.engine.create_execution_context()      assert context.set_optimization_profile_async(         profile_index=profile_index,         stream_handle=stream_handle,     )      self.context = context fixes the problem. This leads me to believe that there is some additional state outside of the execution context that is changed when calling set_optimization_profile_async (e.g. a global symbol?) and causes the output to be broken. Also yes, I am aware of this limitation:  A current exception to this is when using dynamic shapes, when each optimization profile can only have one execution context. docs  This is not the case here as there is a 1to1 mapping between optimization profile <-> execution context.

Environment nvidia docker container 22.12 Relevant Files https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/tree/main/plugin/bertQKVToContextPlugin Steps To Reproduce I have the following code: import torch import torch.nn as nn  # https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/tree/release/8.5/plugin/bertQKVToContextPlugin # The yaml file says that version 3 is not supported yet.  class CustomQKVToContextPluginDynamic(torch.autograd.Function):     @staticmethod     def forward(ctx, input, hidden_size, num_heads):         return input     @staticmethod     def symbolic(g, input, hidden_size, num_heads):         return g.op("CustomQKVToContextPluginDynamic", input, plugin_version_s='1', type_id_i=0, hidden_size_i=hidden_size, num_heads_i=num_heads, has_mask_i=False)  class MyModule(nn.Module):     def __init__(self, hidden_size, num_heads):         super().__init__()         assert hidden_size % num_heads == 0         self.hidden_size = hidden_size         self.num_heads = num_heads         self.size_per_head = hidden_size // num_heads         self.Wq = nn.Linear(self.hidden_size, self.hidden_size)         self.Wk = nn.Linear(self.hidden_size, self.hidden_size)         self.Wv = nn.Linear(self.hidden_size, self.hidden_size)     def forward(self, x):         # title: How to use INT8 quantization in plugin while saving GPU memory?
author: LitLeo
body: Description Environment TensorRT Version:  TensorRT 7.2.x NVIDIA GPU: T4 NVIDIA Driver Version:  Driver Version: 450.119.03 CUDA Version: CUDA10.2 I want to use INT8 quantization in MoE plugin to save GPU memory. The MoE plugin has a lot of weights. There are two ways to pass weight into plugin, (1)quantize weights first and add_constant(like onnx parser) and plugin's  member variable(like embLayerNormPlugin in TRTOOS) The first way, add_constant dose not support INT8 weights because TRT performs the weights quantization itself. (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/unable-to-load-parse-onnx-network-with-int8-operations/170582/2) The second way has the problem of not releasing the GPU memory in time. body: Description Currently in this  demo-diffusion.py , the VAE model conversion of StableDiffusion is only supported for VAE Decoder. Therefore, only the Text2Image pipeline is supported in this program. In daily use, the Image2Image pipeline is also often needed. I made some modifications based on the  demo-diffusion.py , added the Image2Image part, and made some modifications to the model conversion and inference program. At present, the conversion has been successfully completed and a goodresult image has been obtained. Can I submit this modification to the current demo? Some modifications  The VAE class in models.py is divided into two classes: VAEEncoder and VAEDecoder Add add_noise method to scheduler in utilities.py Add an optional memory_pool_limits parameter to the Engine build method in utilities.py Make some changes in demo-diffusion.py  to support image2image inference, such as adjusting timesteps according to strength, adding init_image, strength and other parameters to infer  Rest of the items:   Additionally, I found while using this script that it might be convenient to have an optional transformation of the model. For example, many times we may just want to convert the Unet model with different parameters, but keep the VAE or CLIP unchanged. It seems more convenient to provide an optional name parameter for select conversion.   When force_export is true, maybe you want to re-export the onnx model, but the existence of onnx_opt_path will make it impossible to re-export and optimize onnx. Does this logic need to be modified, when force_export is true, should the onnx model be forcibly exported even if the file exists.   Relevant Files demo/diffusion

author: chavinlo
body: Is it possible to allow for Dynamic Token Length in the compiled CLIP? This would allow for prompt extension as seen in the LPW pipeline in the diffusers repository: https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/main/examples/community/lpw_stable_diffusion.py My current approach to this is just setting a higher text_maxlen on https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/blob/main/demo/Diffusion/models.py#L647 Unfortunately, the longer the compiled token length is, the less attention there is to the prompt if its too short because of the leftover tokens. Example:  (Multipliers) 77 Tokens * X Prompt Extensions ex.: 2nd Image 77 Tokens * 10 Prompt Extensions = 770 Total Tokens You can see that the more Prompt Extensions we use, the more the generated image losses it's charm. Allowing dynamic token length would allow to avoid this problem by only generating the required tokens for the prompt.
